title: What is known about 1RB0RB_1RC0LE_1LD1LA_---0LC_1RF1LE_1RA0RA
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0RB_1RC0LE_1LD1LA_---0LC_1RF1LE_1RA0RA.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The tape is a list of even blocks of 1s; at the left wall the leftmost block is halved again and again (the machine halts if it ever reaches 2, i.e. if a chain starts from a power of two), then a long sweep redistributes the blocks; open, number-theoretic.

Lean proves the halving at the wall for every block size and every tape (halve_W), that a chain starting from a power of two halts (W_pow_halts), that a chain from 2j·q stops at q, and that the blank tape reaches the wall shape; also no halt in the first 107 steps. The long sweep from an odd block back to the wall (the sandpile part) is observation only, so halting is not reduced to a number question in Lean.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (D0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 5,452 cells have been visited and 5,226 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: power/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.279). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.352).

claims.title: 2 shift rules of the sweeps
claims.text: For every n and every tape around: D and C cross 10/01 leftward unchanged. Each is a theorem steps (s·n) … = some … found and proved by tools/py/bbtools/symtm.py.

claims.title: A block of two at the wall halts
claims.text: From E> 0 1 1 0 0 1 0 (a block of two ones at the left wall, in the shape the halvings return to) the machine reaches, in 7 steps, D reading 0, which has no transition; for every tape around.

claims.title: The halving at the wall, for every k and every tape
claims.text: Write W(x, R) for 0^inf E> 0 1^x 0 0 1 0 R (the head at the left wall, a block of x ones, then the separator 0 0 1 0). For every k ≥ 2 and every tape R, W(2k, R) reaches W(k, 1^k 0 R): the block is cut into two halves. Proved as k − 2 rounds (each moves one 1 to the left half and one 1 past the gap) and a last round from a block of 4; the rounds are generated by symtm, the induction is by hand.

claims.title: A halving chain from a power of two halts
claims.text: For every j ≥ 1 and every tape R, the machine started from W(2j, R) halts: j − 1 halvings bring it to W(2, R′), which halts 8 steps later (bbchallenge count).

claims.title: A halving chain from 2<sup>j</sup>·q stops at q
claims.text: For every q ≥ 2, j and R, W(2jq, R) reaches some W(q, R′). So a chain that starts from 2j times an odd number q ≥ 3 reaches the wall with the odd block q, without halting on the way.

claims.title: The run from blank tape reaches the wall shape
claims.text: After 8 steps from blank tape the machine is in W(1, blank) (E at the left wall, a block of one 1).

claims.title: No power of two in the first 121 chains
claims.text: In the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps the run starts 121 halving chains (values up to about 1,900); none starts at a power of two ≥ 2. The number of halvings per chain is distributed like the 2-adic valuation of random integers (63, 32, 14, 8, 3, 1 chains with 0…5 halvings).

claims.title: Halting = a chain starting at a power of two
claims.text: The machine halts if some wall configuration W(x, R) of the run has x a power of two (a theorem, above). The converse (no other way to halt) is heuristic: the 5-cell closed tape language (trusted) allows a halt only in the shape at the end of a chain, and the run is observed to reach every wall in the shape W(x, R), but the long sweep from W(odd, R) to the next wall is not proved. The chain starts look random and grow, so the expected number of powers of two hit converges: probably nonhalting, unproved.

claims.title: Where a halt can happen (closed tape language, 5-cell windows)
claims.text: The closure search of bbtools.ctl with windows of 5 cells is closed but allows halts; the halting abstract configurations constrain the neighbourhood of a halt: a halt (D reading 0) needs the head at the left wall: one 1 to its left and blank tape beyond, 01010/01011 to the right (only 2 of the abstract configurations can halt). This is the halt at x = 2 of the halving chains. A Python check, not a Lean certificate (the Lean library only has the right-edge and no-halt corollaries, which do not apply).

claims.title: Macro structure: halving at the wall, sandpile of even blocks
claims.text: Almost the whole tape is a list of blocks of 1s separated by single 0s: 1^2 0 1^6 0 1^4 0 1^10 0 1^20 0 1^40 0 1^76 0 1^46 0 1^16 0 1^4 0 1^2 0 1^2 0 … 1^2 0. The blocks have even lengths, and the right end is a growing tail of 1^2 0 blocks (right extent ~ t0.35; the left end barely moves: 223 cells after 109 steps).

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. Halting is (heuristically) equivalent to a chain starting at a power of two. The 5-cell closed language agrees on where: it allows a halt only at the left wall, D reading 0 with one 1 to its left and blank beyond. If the chain starts behave like random numbers of size N, the chance of a power of two is about log₂N/N per chain, and the starts grow, so the expected number of hits converges: probably never halts, but nothing here proves it.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. Started on a blank tape, this Turing machine has run for 10<sup>9</sup> steps without stopping. This page runs the real machine in your browser, shows the shape of its run, and lists what is known, each result marked by what it rests on.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator; 5,452 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
Proved in Lean: a halving chain at the wall that starts from a power of two ends in a halt.
The growth shape of the two sides of the tape (see below).

sections.heading: What the machine does: halving at the wall, sandpile of even blocks
html: Almost the whole tape is a list of blocks of 1s separated by single 0s: 1^2 0 1^6 0 1^4 0 1^10 0 1^20 0 1^40 0 1^76 0 1^46 0 1^16 0 1^4 0 1^2 0 1^2 0 … 1^2 0. The blocks have even lengths, and the right end is a growing tail of 1^2 0 blocks (right extent ~ t0.35; the left end barely moves: 183 cells left of the start after 109 steps).

Halving. When the head comes back to the left end in state E, the tape there reads E> 0 1^x 0 0 1 0 … (call it W(x)). If x = 2k is even, the machine cuts the block into two halves and returns to the same shape with x = k: E> 0 1^(2k) 0 0 1 0 R → E> 0 1^k 0 0 1 0 1^k 0 R. In the run: x = 80 → 40 → 20 → 10 → 5 (steps 252,861 to 260,127). This is a Lean theorem for every k ≥ 2 and every tape R (halve_W).

How it cuts: a growing block forms at the wall, and each round the head walks into the big block in pairs of cells, takes two 1s off it, puts one on the wall block and one at the start of the block after the gap 00:

0^inf 1^j E> 0 1^(2m+6) 0 0 1^p …   →   0^inf 1^(j+1) E> 0 1^(2m+4) 0 0 1^(p+1) …

After k − 2 rounds the big block has 4 ones left; a last round gives the wall block its last two 1s and writes the separator 0 0 1 0 again. Two halves of k, one on each side of the separator.

The halt. For x = 2 the halving does not happen: the machine halts 8 steps later (D reads 0). So a chain of halvings that starts from x = 2j (j ≥ 1) ends in a halt — proved in Lean for any tape to the right (W_pow_halts). One that starts from 2j·q, q odd and q > 1, stops at q (also proved, W_chain), and the head leaves on a long rightward sweep, which merges and shifts the blocks (the sandpile-like part: 1^8 0 1^4 0 1^4 becomes 1^10 0 1^8 0 1^2) before coming back with a new x.

In the first 109 steps there are 121 chains; their starting values grow irregularly to about 1,800 (1, 5, 6, 7, 17, 14, 18, 12, 41, 37, 51, 76, 46, 80, …, 1635, 1413, 1258, 749) and none is a power of two. The number of halvings per chain (the 2-adic valuation of the start) is distributed like that of random integers (0: 63, 1: 32, 2: 14, 3: 8, 4: 3, 5: 1).

sections.heading: What a halt would require
html: A halting chain is a sure halt: if the head ever arrives at the wall with a block of 2j ones, the machine stops (a theorem). The converse, that this is the only way to stop, is supported by the 5-cell closed tape language (a trusted computation, not Lean): it allows a halt only at the left wall, D reading 0 with one 1 to its left and blank beyond, which is exactly the end of a chain. What is missing for a full reduction is the rule of the long sweep from W(odd) to the next wall.

If the chain starts behave like random numbers of size N, the chance of a power of two is about log₂N/N per chain, and the starts grow, so the expected number of hits converges: probably never halts, but nothing here proves it.

sections.heading: What is proved, and what is not
html:
• Halving (lean/Halving.lean, kernel): halve_W (W(2k) → W(k) for every k ≥ 2 and every tape), W_pow_halts (W(2j) halts), W_chain (W(2jq) → W(q)), blank_to_W1 (blank tape reaches W(1) in 8 steps). The rounds come from symtm (lean/HalvingRules.lean), the induction is by hand.
  • Sweeps (lean/Sweeps.lean, kernel): D and C cross 10/01 leftward unchanged; for every number of copies and every tape around.
  • Rules (lean/Rules.lean, kernel): two_to_halt, two_stuck.
  • Bounded run (lean/Blank.lean): no halt in 107 steps (native), 10,000 (kernel); the halting transition is the only way to stop.
Not proved: the sweep from an odd block back to the wall, so neither the sequence of chain starts nor “halts only at the end of a chain” is a theorem. Nothing here decides halting.

sections.heading: What would move it forward
html: Find the rule of the sweeps (block list → block list). The rightward sweep after an odd chain end shifts each block across by a zig-zag that moves two 1s per round (1^a 0 1^(2i) 0 B> 1^(b−2i)), and the bounces at the right end add a block 1^2 0 and send a leftward carry that redistributes the middle blocks. With that rule written as a map on block lists and proved like the halving, halting becomes “the orbit hits a power of two at the wall”.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.279). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.352).
After 109 steps the tape spans 5,452 cells (183 left of the start, 4,216 right), with a density of 1s of 0.959.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

summary: The tape is a list of even blocks of 1s; at the left wall the leftmost block is halved again and again (the machine halts if it ever reaches 2, i.e. if a chain starts from a power of two), then a long sweep redistributes the blocks; open, number-theoretic.
